Leverage of the Observations in a Distributional Regression

Source: R/leverage.R
statmod_leverage.Rd

Returns, for each observation \(i\), the block \(H_{ii}\) of the hat matrix of the fit over the coefficients of all the equations. For a model with one equation it is the usual leverage; for a model with \(d\) equations it is a \(d \times d\) matrix, and its trace is the number of effective parameters that observation \(i\) uses.

Usage

statmod_leverage(fit, information = NULL)

Arguments

fit

A StatmodFit().

information

NULL (the default), which is distributions7::expected_info() with the closed form of the family, or an object from distributions7::expected_info() or distributions7::observed_info(). The default does not depend on the information that vcov.StatmodFit() resolves for the family.

Value

A list with blocks, an array of dimension \(n \times d \times d\) of the matrices \(H_{ii}\), leverage, the \(n \times d\) matrix of their diagonals with the equations as columns, and trace, the vector of the traces, and clipped, the number of observations whose information had a negative eigenvalue set to zero (always zero with the expected information). The \(d\) equations are those that have coefficients. Coordinates whose variance is missing (aliased, or held at zero by a penalty) are not part of \(Z_i\).

Details

Let \(\hat\beta\) be the stacked coefficients of the equations that have coefficients, of length \(P\). Write \(Z_i\) for the \(d \times P\) matrix whose row \(a\) holds the row of the design of equation \(a\) for observation \(i\), in the columns of that equation. The score of observation \(i\) in the coefficients is \(u_i = Z_i' s_i\), where \(s_i\) is the vector of the derivatives of its log-likelihood in the \(d\) predictors (on the link scale of each parameter), multiplied by the prior weight. Let \(W_i\) be the \(d \times d\) information of the observation in those predictors, times the prior weight, and \(K\) the penalized information \(\sum_i Z_i' W_i Z_i + S\) that the Bayesian variance \(V_b = K^{-1}\) inverts, with \(S\) the Hessian of the penalty. The linearized fit satisfies \(W^{-1/2}\hat s \approx (I - H)\, W^{-1/2} s\), with the hat matrix $$H = W^{1/2} Z K^{-1} Z' W^{1/2},$$ where \(Z\) stacks the \(Z_i\), \(W\) is block diagonal in the \(W_i\) and \(W^{1/2}\) is the symmetric square root. The diagonal block of observation \(i\) is $$H_{ii} = W_i^{1/2} Z_i K^{-1} Z_i' W_i^{1/2}.$$ It is symmetric, and for an unpenalized fit with \(W\) the information at the estimate it is a projection, so that \(\sum_i \mathrm{tr}\, H_{ii} = P\). With penalties the sum is the effective degrees of freedom.

For a Gaussian linear model with a constant scale and the expected information, the block of the mean equation is the scalar \(h_i = x_i'(X'X)^{-1}x_i\) of stats::hatvalues(). For one equation of a larger model, the diagonal element \((a, a)\) of the block is the leverage that plot_influence() computes for that equation, provided that information is distributions7::expected_info(), the default. Both read \(K^{-1}\) and not the Bayesian variance of vcov.StatmodFit(), which for a coordinate that the marginal criterion estimates holds the curvature of that criterion.

The matrix \(W_i\) and the matrix \(K\) are both read on information. With distributions7::expected_info() the hat matrix is a projection and its trace is \(P\) when there is no penalty. With distributions7::observed_info() the matrix \(W_i\) is the observed information of the observation, which can be indefinite; its root is then the symmetric square root of the positive part (the eigenvalues that are not positive are set to zero, with a zero pseudo-inverse), clipped counts the observations where that happened, and the trace is close to \(P\) but not equal to it. With prior weights \(w_i\) the block is the one of the row as a unit, \(w_i\) times the block of one of its copies.

References

Hoaglin, D. C. and Welsch, R. E. (1978). The hat matrix in regression and ANOVA. The American Statistician, 32(1), 17–22.

See also

hc2_sandwich(), which uses the blocks; plot_influence().

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(60))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
lv <- statmod_leverage(fit)
range(lv$leverage[, "mu"] - hatvalues(lm(y ~ x, dd)))
#> [1] -1.804112e-16  1.387779e-17
